The stops are not caused by the temps, and neither the firmware nor the film alone explains the tripling. The rise comes from the combination: the 30 pallet robots upgraded to firmware 6.4 in Zones A/B went from about 3 to about 16 stops per 100 robot-hours, while the 8 pallet robots still on 6.3 in the same zones stayed flat, and the 6.4 tote robots in Zone C stayed flat. A bench test showed 6.4 treats short specular reflections from the new gloss stretch film as obstacles (17 of 20 stops), while 6.4 with the old matte film gave 0 of 20. Temps arrived in the same lanes and the flat 6.3 robots show they did not drive the rise. Confidence is moderate-to-high, and the bench test is small. Next: switch outbound pallets back to the matte film, keep the current firmware, and track stops by zone and firmware group weekly. Do not adopt the three-strike policy or shorten the protective fields, and do not wait for the December release, which has not been tested against this film. Check the 6.3 security deadline on 31 October.

The stop increase comes from the firmware upgrade and the new gloss stretch film acting together. It does not come from the temps. Firmware 6.4 keeps weak short-range returns that 6.3 discarded. At oblique angles the gloss film throws those returns back, and 6.4 treats them as obstacles. A bench test with no people present showed 17 of 20 stops for 6.4 with gloss film. The other three combinations gave 0 or 1 stops out of 20. In the field, only upgraded pallet robots in the outbound pallet zones (A and B) rose, from 3.2 to 15.6 stops per 100 robot-hours. Pallet robots still on 6.3 in the same zones stayed flat at about 3.1 to 3.3, and so did the tote robots in Zone C. Nearly all the extra stops had no person nearby, and temps were spread across all zones, including Zone C. I'm fairly confident, though only one bench test and one site's telemetry back this.  What to do now: - Switch outbound pallets back to the previous matte film, and track stops by zone and firmware group. - Don't adopt the three-strike policy. It would punish people for stops they didn't cause. - Don't shorten the protective fields. That cuts safety margin and doesn't fix the cause. - Hold off treating the December release as the fix until it's tested against the gloss film. - Treat rolling the 30 upgraded pallet robots back to 6.3 as a fallback only. Security support for 6.3 ends 31 October, so it would need the waiver. - The link between stops and missed cut-offs isn't established. Cut-offs also rose last year with stops flat.

Most of the rise is probably a recording change, not proof that the rota caused more falls. Before the switch, paper forms missed falls: a handover check found three clear unreported falls in six weeks, and the rise is mostly in no-harm and "found on floor" falls. Night falls also look higher, but Q2 night times were partly guessed, and no pre-pilot call-bell data exists. Whether the rota or a shift toward frailer residents adds to the rise is still unknown. The falls rates are inside historical control limits, so this is not yet a clear signal.  I'm moderately confident in the recording finding, less so in the rest. Do not reverse the rota or halt the rollout yet, and do not issue warnings to night carers or withdraw the app, since that would remove better data.  Next: present falls as rates with the reporting change marked, start sampling night call-bell times at both homes, check resident mix and medication changes, and take the rollout decision at a dated late-January review using Q4 data.

A check of Q2 handover notes found three clear unreported falls and three ambiguous ones. The increase is mostly no-harm and unwitnessed falls. Harm falls rose only from 6 to 9.  Second, the rota may be a real factor. Night falls rose, and Ashby Fold's median night call answer time is 3 min 40 s. There is no pre-June baseline, so I can't say calls are slower. Penmor Lodge has no answer-time data at all.  Falls per 1,000 bed days are inside the control limits. Other homes have had similar one-quarter jumps that reversed. But a real 40% increase would take two to three quarters to show.  Medication changes and frailer admissions are untested.  Next steps: keep the pilot running under its existing pause criteria. Show falls as rates, with the recording change marked. Start manual sampling of night call-bell answer times. Review in late January with Q4 data. Don't discipline night staff, and don't withdraw the app.

The longer SME approval times are mainly caused by the valuation stage for property-secured loans, not by staff, Corvane, or the valuation firm. Since the Credit Policy v14 change on 2 May, loans between $150k and $500k must have a full appraisal instead of a desktop valuation. Full appraisals take about 8.6 days at the same firm whose turnaround has not changed, so the valuation stage rose from about 1.7 to 8 days. Unsecured loans, consumer loans on the same system, and underwriting times are essentially unchanged. The headline withdrawal rise is partly an artifact: 32 of the 73 closures since May were automatic 30-day closures for missing document uploads. Next steps: ask the credit risk committee to review the valuation requirement with the measured delay, and add a stage-by-stage breakdown to the dashboard. Hold off on performance plans for new hires, the Corvane payment decision, and fee rebates. Confidence is moderate, because I did not check the policy's risk rationale or the June timing of the valuation jump.

The stops are not caused by the agency temps. They come from a combination of two changes. The 6.4 firmware now keeps weak short-range sensor returns, and the new glossy stretch film produces those returns at oblique angles. Together they make the robots see obstacles that aren't there. Evidence: in the bench test with no people present, 6.4 with gloss film stopped 17 of 20 passes. 6.3 with gloss film stopped 1 of 20, and 6.4 with the old matte film stopped 0 of 20. In the fleet data, only the 6.4 pallet robots in the wrapped-pallet zones rose (3.2 to 15.6 stops per 100 hours). The 6.3 robots working the same zones and shifts stayed flat. The tote robots on 6.4, where no wrapped pallets are staged, also stayed flat. The temps were present for all of these robots, so they do not explain the difference. Confidence is high. What to do: switch back to the previous matte film now, keep the firmware as is, and track stops weekly by zone and firmware group. If the film can't be changed quickly, rolling the pallet robots back to 6.3 is a fallback, but only under the time-limited waiver, because 6.3 security support ends 31 October. Don't shorten the protective fields, and don't adopt the strike policy. Don't count on the December release until it has been tested against this film. The link between stops and missed cut-offs is unproven, since volume rose 18% and cut-off misses also rose last year.

A bench test with no people present showed 17/20 stops for 6.4 with gloss film. The other three combinations gave 1/20, 0/20 and 0/20. Fleet data agrees. Upgraded pallet robots in Zones A/B rose from 3.2 to 15.6 stops per 100 robot-hours, while the 6.3 robots working the same zones stayed flat at about 3.1 to 3.3. Tote robots in Zone C, where no wrapped pallets are staged, were unchanged. Nearly all the added stops had no person nearby, and temps were spread across all zones. I am fairly confident (about 85%). Next steps: switch back to the previous matte film, which restores normal rates without a firmware change, and track stops weekly by zone and firmware group. Roll the 30 pallet robots back to 6.3 only if the film can't be changed quickly. Don't adopt the three-strike policy or the shortened protective fields, because they would punish the wrong people and weaken safety. Test the December release against the gloss film before relying on it.

The evidence doesn't show that the three-person night rota caused the rise in falls, and it doesn't rule it out. Q3 falls (3.7 per 1,000 bed days at both homes) are inside each home's historical range. Q2 was unusually low, near the bottom of each home's range. The app also went live on 1 July, and the Q2 handover-note check found three clear unreported falls and three ambiguous entries in the six weeks that could be checked. That points to Q2 being under-recorded and the app capturing more, especially no-harm and "found on floor" falls. Harm-level falls rose only slightly. Frailer admissions and new GP prescribing are untested. Nobody can say whether call bells are slower, because no pre-June timings exist.  I'd keep the pilot under its existing pause criteria. Re-present falls as rates, with the recording change marked. Start manual sampling of night call-bell response times now. Review the rollout in late January with Q4 data. Reversing the rota now is premature. Warnings to night seniors, or reverting the app to paper, would be harmful. Confidence is moderate. A real rota effect of around 40% could still be hidden, so the January review matters.

The rise in recorded falls at the two homes is real in the figures, but the evidence does not show the rota caused it. Both homes switched to the incident app on 1 July, the same quarter the count jumped. Staff say falls with no injury were under-written before, and a check of old handover notes found at least three unreported falls in a sample of Q2 weeks. Most of the rise is no-harm and 'found on floor' events, which fits better recording. Per bed day, both homes' Q3 rates sit inside their long-run range, and other homes have had similar one-quarter jumps that reversed. However, a real rise of around 40% would take two to three quarters to show, so I can't rule out harm from the rota. Frailer admissions and the GP medication changes are untested. Nobody has call-bell timings from before June, so the claim that bells are answered slower is unproven. I'm moderately confident. Recommended: don't revert or halt the rollout now, and don't discipline staff or withdraw the app. Keep the pilot under its pause criteria. Show falls as rates with the reporting change marked. Start manual sampling of night call-bell response times. Review admissions mix and medication changes. Decide on the rollout at a dated review in late January with Q4 data.
